questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the transformation $T$, where

$$T : w = \frac{1 + z}{1 + 2z}, \quad z \in \mathbb C - \left\{-\tfrac12\right\},$$

from the $z$-plane to the $w$-plane.

Find the invariant points of $T$. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
An invariant point satisfies $w = z$:

$$z = \frac{1 + z}{1 + 2z} \;\Longrightarrow\; z(1 + 2z) = 1 + z \;\Longrightarrow\; z + 2z^2 = 1 + z \;\Longrightarrow\; 2z^2 = 1.$$

So $z = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. Neither value is $-\tfrac12$, so both belong to the domain.

$$\boxed{z = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad z = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}$$

**Check.** For $z = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$: $\dfrac{1 + z}{1 + 2z} = \dfrac{1 + 1/\sqrt2}{1 + \sqrt2} = \dfrac{(\sqrt2 + 1)/\sqrt2}{1 + \sqrt2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ ✓.

Start from $w = \dfrac{1 + z}{1 + 2z}$ and clear the denominator ($z \ne -\tfrac12$):

$$w(1 + 2z) = 1 + z \;\Longrightarrow\; w + 2wz = 1 + z \;\Longrightarrow\; 2wz - z = 1 - w \;\Longrightarrow\; z(2w - 1) = 1 - w.$$

If $w = \tfrac12$ the left side is $0$ while the right side is $\tfrac12 \ne 0$, so $w = \tfrac12$ is never reached; for $w \ne \tfrac12$ we may divide by $2w - 1$:

$$z = \frac{1 - w}{2w - 1}, \quad w \ne \tfrac12. \qquad \blacksquare$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The image of the line $|z| = |z + 2|$ is a circle. Show this and find its centre and radius. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The line.** $|z| = |z + 2|$ says that $z$ is equidistant from $0$ and $-2$: it is the perpendicular bisector of these two points, the line $\operatorname{Re}z = -1$ (with $z = x + iy$: $x^2 + y^2 = (x + 2)^2 + y^2 \Rightarrow x = -1$).

**Substitute $z = \dfrac{1 - w}{2w - 1}$.** We need $z$ and $z + 2$ in terms of $w$:

$$z = \frac{1 - w}{2w - 1}, \qquad z + 2 = \frac{1 - w + 2(2w - 1)}{2w - 1} = \frac{3w - 1}{2w - 1}.$$

The condition $|z| = |z + 2|$ becomes $\dfrac{|1 - w|}{|2w - 1|} = \dfrac{|3w - 1|}{|2w - 1|}$, and since $w \ne \tfrac12$:

$$|w - 1| = |3w - 1|.$$

**Cartesian form.** Let $w = u + iv$. Squaring,

$$(u - 1)^2 + v^2 = (3u - 1)^2 + 9v^2$$

$$u^2 - 2u + 1 + v^2 = 9u^2 - 6u + 1 + 9v^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 8u^2 + 8v^2 - 4u = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; u^2 + v^2 - \tfrac12 u = 0.$$

Complete the square:

$$\left(u - \tfrac14\right)^2 + v^2 = \tfrac{1}{16}.$$

This is a circle in the $w$-plane.

$$\boxed{\text{centre } \left(\tfrac14, 0\right),\quad\text{radius } \tfrac14}$$

The circle passes through $w = 0$ (the image of $z = -1$) and $w = \tfrac12$. The point $w = \tfrac12$ is not an image of any finite $z$ (it corresponds to $z \to \infty$), so the image of the line is this circle without the point $w = \tfrac12$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Sketch the line and the circle on separate axes. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**$z$-plane (the line).** Draw the Argand diagram with real axis $x$ and imaginary axis $y$. The line $|z| = |z + 2|$ is the vertical line $x = -1$, parallel to the imaginary axis, crossing the real axis at $z = -1$, halfway between $z = 0$ and $z = -2$.

**$w$-plane (the circle).** Draw the Argand diagram with axes $u$ (real) and $v$ (imaginary). The circle has centre $\left(\tfrac14, 0\right)$ and radius $\tfrac14$. It crosses the real axis at $u = 0$ (the origin) and at $u = \tfrac12$, and reaches $v = \pm\tfrac14$ above and below its centre. It lies in the half-plane $u \ge 0$ and touches the imaginary axis at the origin. Mark the point $w = \tfrac12$ with an open dot, since it is not an image point.

**Correspondence of points.** $z = -1 \mapsto w = 0$; $z \to \infty$ along the line $\mapsto w \to \tfrac12$. Another point of the line, $z = -1 + i$, gives $w = \dfrac{1 + (-1 + i)}{1 + 2(-1 + i)} = \dfrac{i}{-1 + 2i} = \dfrac{i(-1 - 2i)}{5} = \dfrac{2 - i}{5}$, and $\left(\tfrac25 - \tfrac14\right)^2 + \tfrac{1}{25} = \tfrac{9}{400} + \tfrac{16}{400} = \tfrac{25}{400} = \tfrac{1}{16}$ ✓, so this point lies on the circle.

questions.enonce_markdown: Shade the region on the $z$-plane that maps to the interior of the circle. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
From part (iii), $|w - 1| = |z|\,|2w - 1|$ and $|3w - 1| = |z + 2|\,|2w - 1|$, and the circle is the set where $|3w - 1|^2 - |w - 1|^2 = 0$, that is $8u^2 + 8v^2 - 4u = 0$.

**Interior of the circle.** $\left(u - \tfrac14\right)^2 + v^2 < \tfrac{1}{16}$, equivalently $8u^2 + 8v^2 - 4u < 0$, equivalently

$$|3w - 1|^2 < |w - 1|^2 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; |z + 2|^2\,|2w - 1|^2 < |z|^2\,|2w - 1|^2 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; |z + 2| < |z|.$$

**In the $z$-plane.** $|z + 2| < |z|$ means $z$ is closer to $-2$ than to $0$, so $\operatorname{Re}z < -1$: the open half-plane to the left of the line $x = -1$.

**Check with a point.** $z = -2$ lies in this half-plane and maps to $w = \dfrac{1 - 2}{1 - 4} = \dfrac13$, and $\left|\tfrac13 - \tfrac14\right| = \tfrac{1}{12} < \tfrac14$: inside the circle ✓. A point on the other side, $z = 1$, maps to $w = \dfrac23$ and $\left|\tfrac23 - \tfrac14\right| = \tfrac{5}{12} > \tfrac14$: outside ✓.

**Answer.** On the $z$-plane, shade the half-plane $\operatorname{Re}z < -1$ (everything to the left of the vertical line $x = -1$); draw the line itself dashed, since it maps to the circle and is not part of the interior.
